parole.significato: A title borne by rulers of the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom.
parole.testo: From Middle Persian [Term?] (literally “king of the Kushans”) (modern Persian: کوشانشاه (kūšānšāh /kušânšâh)). By surface analysis, Kushan + shah.

parole.significato: the title of the military commander or commander-in-chief in Sassanian-era Persia
parole.testo: From Middle Persian 𐭮𐭯𐭠𐭧𐭯𐭲𐭩 (spʾḥpty /⁠spāhbed⁠/). Doublet of sparapet.

parole.significato: Any of a collection of hymns and prayers.
parole.testo: From Middle Persian yšt' (yašt, “prayer, worship”), probably from Avestan 𐬫𐬀𐬱𐬙𐬀 (yašta, “honored”), from 𐬫𐬀𐬰 (yaz, “to worship, honor”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁yaǵ-.

parole.significato: An Islamic book that tabulates parameters used for various astronomical events and movements.
A kind of cap from Turkic countries, with a high crown.
parole.testo: From Ottoman Turkish قلپاق (Turkish kalpak), from Proto-Turkic or from Middle Persian kwlʾp̄k' (kulāfak, “little cap; calyx”), diminutive of kwlʾp̄ (kulāf, “cap, bonnet”), (Persian کلاهک (kolâhak), diminutive of کلاه (kolâh, “hat”)), or from Proto-Common Turkic *kalpak. Doublet of kolpik.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient Central Asian tribe; later, a member of the ruling dynasty and people of the Kushan Empire.
parole.testo: From Sanskrit कुषाण (kuṣāṇa) via Hindi कुषाण (kuṣāṇ), or from Middle Persian [script needed] (kušān /⁠kwšn⁠/), either way from Bactrian Κοϸανο (Košano), ultimately from Chinese 貴霜／贵霜 (Guìshuāng) (compare Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit guṣāṇa). parole.significato: A unit of weight in south and west Asia, whose value varies widely by location.
parole.testo: From Hindi मन (man) / Urdu من (man), and their source, Persian من, from Middle Persian, from Akkadian 𒈠𒉡𒌑 (manû). The -d is probably from assimilation with Etymology 1 above, or from comparison with pound.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: The probability of a negative outcome to a decision or event.
parole.testo: From earlier risque, from Middle French risque, from Old Italian risco (“risk”) (modern Italian rischio) and rischiare (“to run into danger”).
